group.basic.label: Basic and beginner-friendly filaments
group.engineering.label: Engineering and heavy-duty filaments
group.flexible.label: Flexible and specialty filaments
chamber.off: Chamber heating OFF, door may stay closed
entry.pla.name: PLA
entry.pla.summary: The easiest material to print: dimensionally accurate and odourless. Stiff, but brittle and sensitive to heat.
entry.pla.printTips: Prints without trouble on an open printer. In an enclosed printer it easily jams in the cold end (heat creep): keep chamber heating OFF, leave the door and top lid open, and keep the inside below 35 °C. Bed 55–60 °C, 100% cooling after the first layer.
entry.pla.dryTips: 50 °C, 4–6 hours – any hotter and the spool may soften. If your dryer's lowest setting is above 50 °C, dry for a shorter time and keep an eye on it. In a multi-zone dryer a material that needs more heat can run in the other zone.
entry.pla.cons.0: softens above about 55 °C (deforms in a car or in the sun)
entry.petg.name: PETG
entry.petg.summary: A tough everyday functional material that resists chemicals and moisture; the happy medium between PLA and ABS.
entry.petg.plate: Textured PEI; on smooth PEI use glue stick AS A RELEASE AGENT
entry.petg.printTips: Prints without trouble on an open printer in a draught-free place. On a printer with a heated chamber keep chamber heating OFF; in an enclosed printer the door can stay closed, but open it if the inside climbs above 45 °C. Cooling 30–60%, more for bridges.
entry.petg.dryTips: 65 °C, 6–8 hours – stringing is usually moisture, not a settings problem. If your dryer cannot reach 65 °C, dry for longer at its highest setting.
entry.petg.uses.2: objects in contact with liquids, planters
entry.petg.cons.0: prone to stringing, especially when damp
entry.petg.cons.1: can stick too hard to smooth PEI
entry.petg.cons.3: bridges and overhangs are weaker than with PLA
entry.abs.name: ABS
entry.abs.summary: A classic engineering plastic: tough, heat-resistant, and can be smoothed and glued with acetone. Prints reliably in a warm, enclosed space.
entry.abs.plate: Textured PEI; for large footprints add glue and a brim
entry.abs.printTips: On a printer with a heated chamber: chamber 60–65 °C, bed 100–105 °C, 10–15 minutes of preheating. In an enclosed but unheated printer, close the door, preheat the inside for 15–20 minutes with the bed at 100–110 °C, and start with smaller parts. On an open printer it will most likely warp and crack. Cooling for bridges only. Styrene emissions: print with the door closed and the printer's filter on, and ventilate the room.
entry.abs.dryTips: 80 °C, 4–6 hours. If your dryer cannot reach 80 °C, dry for longer at its highest setting; ABS is less moisture-sensitive and a freshly opened spool may print without drying.
entry.abs.props.2: easy to machine, sand and glue
entry.abs.props.3: can be smoothed to a gloss with acetone vapour
entry.abs.cons.0: shrinks a lot – without a chamber it warps and cracks
entry.abs.cons.2: yellows and turns brittle under UV
entry.pa-cf.name: PA6-CF / PA12-CF
entry.pa-cf.summary: One of the strongest, stiffest materials available to hobbyists: carbon-fibre nylon that can replace metal, with heat resistance above 150 °C.
entry.pa-cf.printTips: Nozzle 280–300 °C, bed 90–100 °C – you need a printer whose nozzle reaches at least 300 °C. On a printer with a heated chamber: chamber 55–65 °C; in an enclosed but unheated printer, print with the door closed and the inside preheated. Abrasive: only with a hardened steel (or harder) nozzle and drive gear.
entry.pa-cf.dryTips: 85 °C, 10–12 hours – unusable without drying. If your dryer cannot reach 85 °C, dry for much longer at its highest setting, and feed it from the dryer or a dry box while printing too.
entry.pa-cf.props.2: hardly warps thanks to the fibre
entry.pa-cf.cons.0: Abrasive: only with a hardened steel (or harder) nozzle and drive gear – check that the nozzle and drive gear you use are hardened.
group.basic.blurb: PLA, PETG and their variants – most prints are made from these. They work best without a heated chamber, with the door open.
group.engineering.blurb: ABS/ASA, nylons, polycarbonate, fiber-reinforced composites. A heated chamber and a dryer really matter here.
group.flexible.blurb: TPUs, dissolvable and breakaway support materials, special-purpose materials. Multiple independent heads help most here.
sub.Mechanikailag erősített és ipari PLA: Mechanically reinforced and industrial PLA variants
rule.0.title: Chamber: not every material suits it
rule.0.text: PLA, PVA, TPU: chamber heating OFF and door/lid open (below 35 °C). PETG: heating OFF, a closed door is still fine. ABS/ASA/PA/PC: 55–65 °C, with 10–20 minutes of preheating.
rule.1.title: Nozzle: the machine's maximum matters
rule.1.text: Everything goes comfortably up to 300 °C (PA-CF, PC, PET-CF). PPA-CF and PPS-CF need a nozzle around 300 °C or higher; PEEK/PEI won't run on a typical desktop machine. Fiber-reinforced, glow and metal-filled materials need a hardened nozzle.
rule.2.title: Multiple independent heads: by material family
rule.2.text: If the machine has several independent heads: switching heads leaves no purge waste, so PLA↔PETG interface layers, dissolvable supports and rigid+flexible combinations are cheap. It's worth keeping one head with a hardened nozzle for abrasive materials.
rule.3.title: Drying: the temperature differs by material
rule.3.text: PLA/PVA/PVB 50 °C · PETG/PCTG/HIPS 65 °C · TPU 70 °C · ABS/ASA 80 °C · PA/PC/PET-CF 85 °C. Where the manufacturer asks for over 100 °C (PC, PPA, PPS) and your dryer can't reach it, expect a longer drying time. Nylon, PC, TPU and PVA should run from the dryer during printing too.
entry.pctg.name: PCTG
entry.pctg.summary: PCTG is a tougher, clearer relative of PETG – better impact resistance and layer adhesion, with similarly easy printing.
entry.pctg.plate: Textured PEI; release agent on smooth PEI
entry.pctg.printTips: As with PETG: chamber heating OFF, medium cooling. On thick walls, slow down for clarity.
entry.pctg.props.0: much higher impact strength than PETG
entry.pctg.cons.1: heat resistance is the same as PETG (~75 °C)
entry.pla-plus.name: PLA+ / Tough PLA
entry.pla-plus.summary: PLA toughened with additives: less brittle, handles impact and screwing better, while printing just as easily.
entry.pla-plus.printTips: In an enclosed printer, PLA easily gets stuck on the cold side (heat creep): chamber heating OFF, door and top cover open, chamber kept below 35 °C. Prefers a nozzle 5–10 °C warmer than plain PLA.
entry.pla-plus.dryTips: 50 °C – warmer than this the spool may soften. If your dryer's lowest setting is above 50 °C, dry for a shorter time and keep watch. In a two-zone dryer, a material that needs a higher temperature can run in the other zone.
entry.pla-plus.cons.0: heat resistance no better than PLA
entry.pla-plus.cons.1: recipes vary greatly between manufacturers – no standard
entry.hs-pla.name: High-Speed PLA
entry.hs-pla.summary: High-flow PLA for fast machines: melts cleanly even at a higher volumetric flow, so the fast profile doesn't cost quality.
entry.hs-pla.printTips: In an enclosed printer, PLA easily gets stuck on the cold side (heat creep): chamber heating OFF, door and top cover open, chamber kept below 35 °C. This is where the machine's acceleration pays off: calibrate the max. volumetric flow (per head, with several heads).
entry.hs-pla.dryTips: 50 °C – warmer than this the spool may soften. If your dryer's lowest setting is above 50 °C, dry for a shorter time and keep watch. In a two-zone dryer, a material that needs a higher temperature can run in the other zone.
entry.hs-pla.props.0: stable up to 25–30 mm³/s volumetric flow
entry.hs-pla.cons.0: at very high speed the surface is more matte and layer adhesion is weaker
entry.pla-cf.name: PLA-CF
entry.pla-cf.summary: PLA filled with chopped carbon fiber: stiffer, more dimensionally stable, matte, with an “engineering” finish – layer lines almost disappear.
entry.pla-cf.printTips: In an enclosed printer, PLA easily gets stuck on the cold side (heat creep): chamber heating OFF, door and top cover open, chamber kept below 35 °C. Abrasive: only with a hardened steel (or harder) nozzle and gears – check that the nozzle and gears you use are hardened.
entry.pla-cf.cons.2: Abrasive: only with a hardened steel (or harder) nozzle and gears – check that the nozzle and gears you use are hardened.
entry.ht-pla.name: HT-PLA (heat-resistant PLA)
entry.ht-pla.summary: PLA that can be crystallized by heat treatment (annealing): after printing, treated at about 80–100 °C, it reaches heat resistance above 100 °C.
entry.ht-pla.printTips: In an enclosed printer, PLA easily gets stuck on the cold side (heat creep): chamber heating OFF, door and top cover open, chamber kept below 35 °C. Heat treatment is NOT best done in the printer's chamber (its temperature is too low).
entry.ht-pla.dryTips: Drying at 55 °C. Heat treatment at 80–85 °C, 1–2 hours, with slow cooling – in the dryer's annealing mode if it reaches this temperature, otherwise in an oven (the manufacturer may ask for 90–100 °C – then you need an oven).
entry.ht-pla.uses.0: indoor parts exposed to sun or car interiors
entry.ht-pla.cons.0: shrinks/warps during heat treatment (1–3%) – must be compensated in advance
entry.ht-pla.cons.1: without heat treatment it's plain PLA
entry.silk-pla.name: Silk PLA
entry.silk-pla.summary: High-gloss, silk-look decorative PLA – the sheen almost hides the layer lines.
entry.silk-pla.printTips: In an enclosed printer, PLA easily gets stuck on the cold side (heat creep): chamber heating OFF, door and top cover open, chamber kept below 35 °C. Outer walls at 40–60 mm/s and 220–230 °C give the best shine.
entry.silk-pla.dryTips: 50 °C – warmer than this the spool may soften. If your dryer's lowest setting is above 50 °C, dry for a shorter time and keep watch. In a two-zone dryer, a material that needs a higher temperature can run in the other zone.
entry.silk-pla.props.1: nice surface even at large layer heights
entry.silk-pla.cons.0: weak layer adhesion, brittle – not a functional material
entry.silk-pla.cons.1: loses its sheen when printed fast
entry.silk-pla.cons.2: prone to clogging if too cold
entry.matte-pla.name: Matte PLA
entry.matte-pla.summary: PLA matted with a mineral additive: velvety, non-reflective surface that hides layer lines.
entry.matte-pla.printTips: In an enclosed printer, PLA easily gets stuck on the cold side (heat creep): chamber heating OFF, door and top cover open, chamber kept below 35 °C.
entry.matte-pla.dryTips: 50 °C, preferably for 6–8 hours – the matte filler binds more water.
entry.matte-pla.cons.1: more sensitive to moisture than plain PLA
entry.multicolor-pla.name: Dual / Tri-Color PLA
entry.multicolor-pla.summary: Two or three colors side by side, co-extruded into one filament: the object changes color depending on the viewing angle.
entry.multicolor-pla.printTips: In an enclosed printer, PLA easily gets stuck on the cold side (heat creep): chamber heating OFF, door and top cover open, chamber kept below 35 °C. One head is enough; you can fine-tune where the colors land by rotating the model on the bed.
entry.multicolor-pla.dryTips: 50 °C – warmer than this the spool may soften. If your dryer's lowest setting is above 50 °C, dry for a shorter time and keep watch. In a two-zone dryer, a material that needs a higher temperature can run in the other zone.
entry.multicolor-pla.props.0: color-changing effect with a single head
entry.multicolor-pla.cons.0: the effect depends on the filament's orientation – it must run from the spool without twisting
entry.rainbow-pla.name: Rainbow / Gradient PLA
entry.rainbow-pla.summary: PLA whose color changes along the length of the filament: the print gradually shifts color along its height.
entry.rainbow-pla.printTips: In an enclosed printer, PLA easily gets stuck on the cold side (heat creep): chamber heating OFF, door and top cover open, chamber kept below 35 °C. Shows off best on large, tall objects.
entry.rainbow-pla.dryTips: 50 °C – warmer than this the spool may soften. If your dryer's lowest setting is above 50 °C, dry for a shorter time and keep watch. In a two-zone dryer, a material that needs a higher temperature can run in the other zone.
entry.rainbow-pla.cons.0: on small objects the transition barely shows (the color cycle is long)
entry.rainbow-pla.cons.1: the result can't be planned precisely
entry.translucent-pla.name: Translucent / Crystal PLA
entry.translucent-pla.summary: Translucent PLA for lamps, light guides and lithophanes.
entry.translucent-pla.printTips: In an enclosed printer, PLA easily gets stuck on the cold side (heat creep): chamber heating OFF, door and top cover open, chamber kept below 35 °C. For translucency: thick layers, a nozzle 5–10 °C warmer, slow walls, less cooling.
entry.translucent-pla.dryTips: 50 °C – warmer than this the spool may soften. If your dryer's lowest setting is above 50 °C, dry for a shorter time and keep watch. In a two-zone dryer, a material that needs a higher temperature can run in the other zone.
entry.translucent-pla.cons.0: true water clarity can't be achieved with FDM
entry.sparkle-pla.name: Sparkle / Galaxy / Marble PLA
entry.sparkle-pla.summary: PLA filled with glitter or stone-look particles: a grainy, sparkling or marbled surface that covers layers well.
entry.sparkle-pla.nozzleDia: 0.4 mm or larger; hardened for lasting use
entry.sparkle-pla.printTips: In an enclosed printer, PLA easily gets stuck on the cold side (heat creep): chamber heating OFF, door and top cover open, chamber kept below 35 °C. For regular use, put it in a head with a hardened nozzle.
entry.sparkle-pla.dryTips: 50 °C – warmer than this the spool may soften. If your dryer's lowest setting is above 50 °C, dry for a shorter time and keep watch. In a two-zone dryer, a material that needs a higher temperature can run in the other zone.
entry.sparkle-pla.cons.0: the particles slightly wear brass nozzles
entry.wood-pla.name: Wood PLA
entry.wood-pla.summary: PLA filled with wood, bamboo or cork flour: wood feel and smell, sandable and stainable surface.
entry.wood-pla.printTips: In an enclosed printer, PLA easily gets stuck on the cold side (heat creep): chamber heating OFF, door and top cover open, chamber kept below 35 °C. Unload immediately after printing – don't leave it in the hot head. On multi-head prints, lower the temperature of the waiting head.
entry.wood-pla.dryTips: 45–50 °C, 4–6 hours – because of the wood fiber, don't go higher.
entry.wood-pla.props.1: the nozzle temperature can darken the shade
entry.wood-pla.cons.0: clogs easily: the wood fiber burns if it sits in the hot nozzle
entry.glow-pla.name: Glow-in-the-Dark PLA
entry.glow-pla.summary: PLA with strontium-aluminate pigment: it charges up in light and glows in the dark.
entry.glow-pla.printTips: In an enclosed printer, PLA easily gets stuck on the cold side (heat creep): chamber heating OFF, door and top cover open, chamber kept below 35 °C. Abrasive: only with a hardened steel (or harder) nozzle and gears – check that the nozzle and gears you use are hardened. More walls and higher infill are needed for brightness.
entry.glow-pla.dryTips: 50 °C – warmer than this the spool may soften. If your dryer's lowest setting is above 50 °C, dry for a shorter time and keep watch. In a two-zone dryer, a material that needs a higher temperature can run in the other zone.
entry.glow-pla.cons.0: STRONGLY abrasive – destroys a brass nozzle within a few hundred grams
entry.lw-pla.name: Lightweight / Foaming PLA
entry.lw-pla.summary: Heat-foaming PLA: above 230 °C the filament foams, so the same volume weighs a half to a third.
entry.lw-pla.printTips: In an enclosed printer, PLA easily gets stuck on the cold side (heat creep): chamber heating OFF, door and top cover open, chamber kept below 35 °C. Calibrate a temperature–flow tower; instead of retraction, use “avoid crossing walls” and single-wall (vase-like) structures.
entry.lw-pla.dryTips: 50 °C – warmer than this the spool may soften. If your dryer's lowest setting is above 50 °C, dry for a shorter time and keep watch. In a two-zone dryer, a material that needs a higher temperature can run in the other zone. Moist filament foams unpredictably.
entry.lw-pla.props.1: the foaming can be controlled with temperature
entry.lw-pla.cons.0: needs separate calibration: flow 45–65% depending on temperature
entry.metal-pla.name: Metal-filled PLA
entry.metal-pla.summary: PLA filled with real metal powder (bronze, copper, iron): heavy, polishable, patinable.
entry.metal-pla.printTips: In an enclosed printer, PLA easily gets stuck on the cold side (heat creep): chamber heating OFF, door and top cover open, chamber kept below 35 °C. Abrasive: only with a hardened steel (or harder) nozzle and gears – check that the nozzle and gears you use are hardened. It needs a short, straight filament path – brittle filament breaks at sharp bends.
entry.metal-pla.dryTips: 50 °C – warmer than this the spool may soften. If your dryer's lowest setting is above 50 °C, dry for a shorter time and keep watch. In a two-zone dryer, a material that needs a higher temperature can run in the other zone.
entry.metal-pla.cons.0: brittle, the filament breaks easily on the spool
entry.metal-pla.cons.2: expensive per gram because of the high density
entry.colorchange-pla.name: Heat / UV Color-Change PLA
entry.colorchange-pla.summary: PLA made with pigment that changes color with temperature (around 30–45 °C) or UV light.
entry.colorchange-pla.printTips: In an enclosed printer, PLA easily gets stuck on the cold side (heat creep): chamber heating OFF, door and top cover open, chamber kept below 35 °C. Stay in the lower half of the temperature range.
entry.colorchange-pla.dryTips: 45–50 °C – don't dry it warmer, the pigment is sensitive.
entry.colorchange-pla.cons.0: the pigment fades over time under strong UV
entry.colorchange-pla.cons.1: an overly hot nozzle can ruin the effect
entry.conductive-pla.name: Conductive PLA
entry.conductive-pla.summary: PLA filled with carbon black or graphite: for low-current circuits, touch sensors and antistatic objects.
entry.conductive-pla.printTips: In an enclosed printer, PLA easily gets stuck on the cold side (heat creep): chamber heating OFF, door and top cover open, chamber kept below 35 °C. If the machine has several independent heads, it can be combined with other material without purge waste; on a single-head machine, switching needs a purge. This way the conductive track can be printed directly into the insulating PLA body.
entry.conductive-pla.dryTips: 50 °C – warmer than this the spool may soften. If your dryer's lowest setting is above 50 °C, dry for a shorter time and keep watch. In a two-zone dryer, a material that needs a higher temperature can run in the other zone.
entry.conductive-pla.props.1: can be embedded in multi-material prints
entry.conductive-pla.cons.0: not a wire replacement: the resistance is high
entry.petg-hf.name: PETG HF (High-Flow)
entry.petg-hf.summary: High-flow PETG for fast machines – PETG's toughness at speeds close to PLA's.
entry.petg-hf.plate: Textured PEI; release agent on smooth PEI
entry.petg-hf.printTips: Chamber heating OFF. Calibrate the max. volumetric flow; at high speed, 250–260 °C.
entry.petg-hf.cons.0: at the highest speed, layer adhesion is weaker
entry.petg-cf.name: PETG-CF
entry.petg-cf.summary: Carbon-fiber-stiffened PETG: matte, dimensionally stable, a workshop material that is more heat- and impact-resistant than PLA-CF.
entry.petg-cf.printTips: Chamber heating OFF, or at most 40 °C. Abrasive: only with a hardened steel (or harder) nozzle and gears – check that the nozzle and gears you use are hardened.
entry.petg-cf.props.1: matte surface, layer lines barely visible
entry.petg-cf.cons.1: Abrasive: only with a hardened steel (or harder) nozzle and gears – check that the nozzle and gears you use are hardened.
entry.asa.name: ASA
entry.asa.summary: The UV- and weather-resistant relative of ABS: the first choice for outdoor parts.
entry.asa.plate: Textured PEI; brim for large parts
entry.asa.printTips: On a heated-chamber printer: chamber 55–65 °C, bed 100 °C, start with preheating. In an enclosed but unheated printer, print with the door closed and a preheated interior; on an open printer it will warp. Styrene emissions: print with the door closed using the machine's filter, and ventilate.
entry.asa.props.0: excellent UV and weather resistance, doesn't yellow
entry.asa.cons.0: prone to warping without a chamber
entry.abs-gf.name: ABS-GF / ASA-CF
entry.abs-gf.summary: ABS/ASA reinforced with glass or carbon fiber: stiffer, and it warps much less than the unfilled version.
entry.abs-gf.printTips: On a heated-chamber printer: chamber 55–65 °C; in an enclosed but unheated printer, with the door closed and preheated. Abrasive: only with a hardened steel (or harder) nozzle and gears – check that the nozzle and gears you use are hardened. Styrene emissions: print with the door closed using the machine's filter, and ventilate.
entry.abs-gf.cons.1: Abrasive: only with a hardened steel (or harder) nozzle and gears – check that the nozzle and gears you use are hardened.
entry.pc-abs.name: PC-ABS
entry.pc-abs.summary: A blend of polycarbonate and ABS: more heat- and impact-resistant than ABS, and easier to print than pure PC.
entry.pc-abs.printTips: On a heated-chamber printer: chamber as warm as possible (60–65 °C), bed 105–110 °C, long preheating, brim; on an unheated, enclosed printer, try only smaller pieces. For large-footprint parts, round the corners. Styrene emissions: print with the door closed using the machine's filter, and ventilate.
entry.pc-abs.dryTips: 85 °C, 6–8 hours; keep it in the dryer during printing too. If your dryer can't reach 85 °C, dry it at its highest setting.
entry.pc-abs.cons.0: warps – needs a chamber at the upper temperature range
entry.hips.name: HIPS
entry.hips.summary: Light, easily sanded polystyrene; used as a standalone material and as a support for ABS, which dissolves in d-limonene.
entry.hips.printTips: If the machine has several independent heads, it can be combined with other material without purge waste; on a single-head machine, switching needs a purge. On a multi-head machine: ABS in one head and HIPS support in the other, at the same chamber temperature (55–60 °C). Styrene emissions: print with the door closed using the machine's filter, and ventilate.
entry.hips.props.1: light (≈1.04 g/cm³), easily sanded and painted
entry.hips.props.2: prints at the same temperatures as ABS
entry.asa-aero.name: ASA Aero / LW-ASA
entry.asa-aero.summary: Foaming ASA: the lightness of LW-PLA with the heat and UV resistance of ASA – for RC aircraft that sit in the sun.
entry.asa-aero.printTips: On a heated-chamber printer: chamber 45–55 °C; on an unheated, enclosed printer with the door closed. Temperature–flow calibration, single-wall structures. Styrene emissions: print with the door closed using the machine's filter, and ventilate.
entry.asa-aero.props.1: UV- and heat-resistant (doesn't soften in the sun)
entry.pa6.name: PA6 (Nylon 6)
entry.pa6.summary: Tough, wear-resistant, self-lubricating engineering material for gears and sliding parts. Very hygroscopic.
entry.pa6.printTips: On a heated-chamber printer: chamber 55–65 °C, bed 90 °C, adhesive required; in an unheated, enclosed printer with the door closed, preheated, with smaller pieces. Cooling 0–20%.
entry.pa6.dryTips: 85 °C, 8–12 hours. If your dryer can't reach 85 °C, dry it at its highest setting. Keep it running from the dryer during printing too – nylon re-absorbs moisture within hours.
entry.pa6.cons.0: very hygroscopic: when wet it crackles, foams and is weak
entry.pa6.cons.2: softens and changes size after absorbing moisture
entry.pa12.name: PA12 (Nylon 12)
entry.pa12.summary: Absorbs far less water than PA6, is more dimensionally stable and easier to print – in return it's slightly softer.
entry.pa12.printTips: On a heated-chamber printer: chamber 50–60 °C, bed 80–90 °C; in an unheated, enclosed printer it also works with the door closed; on an open printer it may warp.
entry.pa12.dryTips: 80 °C, 8–10 hours. Keep it running from the dryer during printing too – nylon re-absorbs moisture within hours.
entry.pa12.cons.1: lower stiffness and heat resistance than PA6
entry.pa-gf.name: PA6-GF
entry.pa-gf.summary: Glass-fiber nylon: tougher and cheaper than the CF version, slightly less stiff; electrically insulating.
entry.pa-gf.printTips: On a heated-chamber printer: chamber 55–65 °C; in an enclosed but unheated printer, with the door closed and preheated. Abrasive: only with a hardened steel (or harder) nozzle and gears – check that the nozzle and gears you use are hardened.
entry.pa-gf.dryTips: 85 °C, 8–12 hours. Keep it running from the dryer during printing too – nylon re-absorbs moisture within hours.
entry.pa-gf.cons.0: glass fiber is even more abrasive than carbon fiber
entry.ppa-cf.name: PAHT-CF / PPA-CF
entry.ppa-cf.summary: High-temperature (semi-aromatic) carbon-fiber polyamide: absorbs less water, heat-resistant up to 190–230 °C, can replace aluminum.
entry.ppa-cf.printTips: Only with a machine whose nozzle reaches 300–320 °C; choose a type whose recommended range is around 300–310 °C. On a heated-chamber printer: chamber 60–65 °C, bed 100–110 °C.
entry.ppa-cf.dryTips: Manufacturers ask for 100–120 °C; if your dryer only goes up to 85 °C, you need a longer time, 12–16 hours, and it should stay inside during printing too.
entry.ppa-cf.props.2: much lower moisture absorption than PA6
entry.ppa-cf.cons.0: needs a 300–320 °C nozzle – not every machine reaches it
entry.ppa-cf.cons.2: Abrasive: only with a hardened steel (or harder) nozzle and gears – check that the nozzle and gears you use are hardened.
entry.pc.name: PC (polycarbonate)
entry.pc.summary: Extremely impact-resistant, heat-resistant up to 110–130 °C, even transparent technical material. Shrinks strongly, so it needs a chamber and patience.
entry.pc.printTips: A chamber heatable to 60–65 °C is enough for small and medium pieces; large, flat parts will warp. On a heated-chamber printer: chamber as warm as possible, bed 110–115 °C, 20+ minutes of preheating, 0% cooling. To start, choose an “easy-to-print” PC blend.
entry.pc.dryTips: The manufacturer often recommends 100–120 °C; if your dryer only goes to 85 °C, 8–12 hours, and it should stay in the dryer during printing too.
entry.pc.props.3: also available as a flame-retardant (FR) type
entry.pc.cons.0: strong warping and layer separation – the ideal chamber would be 80–100 °C
entry.pc-cf.name: PC-CF
entry.pc-cf.summary: Carbon-fiber-stabilized PC: the fiber holds back shrinkage, so it prints more easily than unfilled PC, and it's even stiffer.
entry.pc-cf.printTips: On a heated-chamber printer: chamber 60–65 °C, bed 110 °C; because of the fiber, this is enough for most sizes here. On an unheated, enclosed printer, preheat and try smaller pieces. Abrasive: only with a hardened steel (or harder) nozzle and gears – check that the nozzle and gears you use are hardened.
entry.pc-cf.props.1: much less warping than pure PC
entry.pc-cf.cons.0: loses part of PC's impact resistance
entry.pc-cf.cons.1: Abrasive: only with a hardened steel (or harder) nozzle and gears – check that the nozzle and gears you use are hardened.
entry.pet-cf.name: PET-CF
entry.pet-cf.summary: Carbon-fiber PET: the stiffness of nylon composites, without dimensional change from moisture – for outdoor and wet environments.
entry.pet-cf.printTips: A chamber is optional (45–60 °C helps with large pieces); bed 80–100 °C. Abrasive: only with a hardened steel (or harder) nozzle and gears – check that the nozzle and gears you use are hardened.
entry.pet-cf.dryTips: 85 °C, 8–10 hours (the manufacturer's recommendation may be 100–120 °C). Heat treatment is also specified at 100–120 °C – that needs an oven; if your dryer only reaches 85 °C, it gives only a partial result.
entry.pet-cf.props.1: absorbs almost no water, dimensionally stable
entry.pet-cf.cons.1: Abrasive: only with a hardened steel (or harder) nozzle and gears – check that the nozzle and gears you use are hardened.
entry.pet-cf.cons.2: full heat resistance requires heat treatment
entry.pp.name: PP (polypropylene) / PP-GF
entry.pp.summary: Chemical-resistant, fatigue-resistant, light material for “living hinges” and chemical containers. One of the hardest-to-adhere, strongly warping filaments.
entry.pp.plate: PP packing tape, or a PP-compatible adhesive sheet/glue
entry.pp.printTips: Difficult because of adhesion, not temperature. On a heated-chamber printer: chamber 45–60 °C, a wide brim or raft, slow first layer. PP-GF is much easier to handle – it needs a hardened nozzle.
entry.pp.dryTips: Barely absorbs moisture: 60–65 °C, 4 hours is enough.
entry.pp.props.2: very light (0.9 g/cm³), doesn't absorb moisture
entry.pp.cons.0: sticks only to PP: needs PP packing tape or a special sheet
entry.pps-cf.name: PPS / PPS-CF
entry.pps-cf.summary: Resistant to almost all chemicals, self-extinguishing, stable above 200 °C. Requires a very high nozzle temperature.
entry.pps-cf.printTips: Only with a machine whose nozzle reaches 310–320 °C, and with a type whose range starts at 310–320 °C; slowly, with small pieces. On a heated-chamber printer: chamber 60–65 °C (less than you'd think), bed 110–120 °C. Full crystallinity requires post heat treatment (in an oven).
entry.pps-cf.dryTips: Manufacturer recommendation 120–130 °C; if your dryer only reaches 85 °C, 12+ hours. Fortunately it absorbs very little water.
entry.pps-cf.cons.0: needs a 310–340 °C nozzle – not every machine reaches it
entry.pps-cf.cons.3: Abrasive: only with a hardened steel (or harder) nozzle and gears – check that the nozzle and gears you use are hardened.
entry.peek.name: PEEK / PEKK / PEI (ULTEM)
entry.peek.summary: Top materials for aerospace and medical technology. For information: they can NOT be printed on typical desktop machines.
entry.peek.printTips: NOT possible on a typical desktop machine: a 360–420 °C nozzle, 120–160 °C bed and 90–150 °C chamber exceed the limits of hobby machines. If such properties are needed: PPA-CF or PPS-CF are the realistic upper limit; above that, use a print service.
entry.peek.dryTips: They need drying at 150 °C – typical dryers aren't suitable for this.
entry.peek.cons.1: several hundred thousand HUF per kilogram
entry.tpu-95a.name: TPU 95A
entry.tpu-95a.summary: The “standard” flexible material: rubber-like, almost impossible to tear, wear-resistant – and still relatively easy to print.
entry.tpu-95a.plate: Textured PEI (sticks too strongly to smooth PEI – needs release agent)
entry.tpu-95a.printTips: Chamber heating OFF, door open. Soft filament: needs a short, straight, low-friction filament path. If the machine's automatic feeder doesn't handle it, thread it from an external spool holder directly into the head. Keep retraction small (0.4–0.8 mm) and slow. If the machine has several independent heads, it can be combined with other material without purge waste; on a single-head machine, switching needs a purge. E.g. a rigid frame + TPU seal in one print.
entry.tpu-95a.dryTips: 70 °C, 6–8 hours; run it from the dryer during long prints.
entry.tpu-95a.cons.1: stringy, retraction helps only to a limited extent
entry.tpu-95a.cons.2: hygroscopic: when wet it blisters and strings
entry.tpu-soft.name: TPU 85A and softer
entry.tpu-soft.summary: A truly soft, rubber-band-like material. The filament is so soft that it easily crumples in the extruder.
entry.tpu-soft.printTips: Difficult to feed: soft filament needs a short, straight, low-friction filament path. If the machine's automatic feeder doesn't handle it, thread it from an external spool holder directly into the head. Retraction off or minimal; reduce the pressure of the filament tensioner.
entry.tpu-soft.dryTips: 65–70 °C, 6–8 hours; keep it in the dryer during printing too.
entry.tpu-soft.cons.1: prints only with direct drive and a guided filament path
entry.tpu-hf.name: TPU HF / hard TPU (64D)
entry.tpu-hf.summary: Fast-printing or harder (60–64D) TPUs that run through automatic feeder systems too.
entry.tpu-hf.printTips: Chamber heating OFF. For multi-material prints this is the most convenient flexible type. If the machine has several independent heads, it can be combined with other material without purge waste; on a single-head machine, switching needs a purge.
entry.tpu-hf.cons.0: at 64D it's more a tough plastic than a rubber
entry.tpe-peba.name: TPE / TPC / PEBA
entry.tpe-peba.summary: Special elastomers: TPC is more chemical- and heat-resistant than TPU, and PEBA is very light and returns energy outstandingly.
entry.tpe-peba.printTips: Difficult to feed; temperature is not the problem. Soft filament: needs a short, straight, low-friction filament path. If the machine's automatic feeder doesn't handle it, thread it from an external spool holder directly into the head.
entry.tpe-peba.uses.2: wearable items in contact with skin
entry.tpe-peba.props.0: PEBA: high energy return, flexible even in the cold, light
entry.tpe-peba.props.1: TPC: better heat and UV resistance
entry.tpe-peba.cons.2: settings vary greatly from material to material
entry.pva.name: PVA
entry.pva.summary: Support material that dissolves completely in water, for PLA: intricate internal cavities, perfect bottom surfaces.
entry.pva.plate: (printed as support onto the main material)
entry.pva.printTips: Ideal with its own head. If the machine has several independent heads, it can be combined with other material without purge waste; on a single-head machine, switching needs a purge. Use it only as the interface layer; the body of the support should be PLA – this uses a fraction of the material. Lower the temperature of the waiting PVA head.
entry.pva.dryTips: 50 °C, 8–12 hours, and print ONLY from the dryer. Storage: airtight, with desiccant.
entry.pva.uses.1: internal channels, closed cavities, moving assemblies
entry.pva.props.0: dissolves without a trace in lukewarm water
entry.pva.cons.0: the most hygroscopic filament: it's ruined within hours in air
entry.pva.cons.1: burns and clogs if it sits in the hot nozzle
entry.bvoh.name: BVOH
entry.bvoh.summary: An improved relative of PVA: dissolves faster, clogs less, and bonds to PETG and ABS too.
entry.bvoh.plate: (printed as support onto the main material)
entry.bvoh.printTips: If the machine has several independent heads, it can be combined with other material without purge waste; on a single-head machine, switching needs a purge. For PETG this is the dissolvable support. It softens in a chamber above 50 °C – for heated-chamber materials, HIPS is better.
entry.bvoh.uses.0: dissolvable support for PLA, PETG, TPU and (to a limited extent) ABS
entry.breakaway.name: Breakaway support / PLA↔PETG interface layer
entry.breakaway.summary: Material pairs that don't stick to each other: a PLA-print with PETG, or a PETG-print with PLA interface layer – zero gap, mirror-smooth bottom surface, no water needed.
entry.breakaway.plate: (printed as support onto the main material)
entry.breakaway.printTips: Its greatest advantage is on a multi-head machine: no purge when switching heads, so the PLA↔PETG interface layer is practically free; on a single-head machine it costs purge waste. In the slicer: only the interface layers should be made of the other material, Z-gap 0, interface spacing 0.
entry.breakaway.dryTips: Dry PETG at 65 °C and PLA at 50 °C; in a two-zone dryer, both can run at once.
entry.breakaway.props.0: no soaking, comes off by hand
entry.breakaway.props.1: printable with a 0 mm support gap
entry.breakaway.props.2: cheap (the PLA/PETG itself is the support)
entry.breakaway.cons.0: can't be removed from a closed internal cavity
entry.breakaway.cons.1: a compromise is needed between the two materials' bed and chamber requirements
entry.pvb.name: PVB
entry.pvb.summary: A material that prints like PLA and can be polished to a glass-smooth finish with isopropyl alcohol vapor or spray.
entry.pvb.printTips: In an enclosed printer, PLA easily gets stuck on the cold side (heat creep): chamber heating OFF, door and top cover open, chamber kept below 35 °C.
entry.pvb.props.0: can be smoothed with IPA (without the dangers of acetone)
entry.pvb.cons.1: heat resistance around that of PLA
entry.esd.name: ESD-safe materials (PETG-ESD, ABS-ESD)
entry.esd.summary: Materials with controlled surface resistance (10⁶–10⁹ Ω) for electronics manufacturing aids: they don't build up charge and don't damage components.
entry.esd.printTips: The settings follow the base material: PETG-ESD without a chamber, ABS-ESD with a heated chamber (60–65 °C). Abrasive: only with a hardened steel (or harder) nozzle and gears – check that the nozzle and gears you use are hardened.
entry.esd.props.1: the mechanical properties of the base material (PETG/ABS)
entry.esd.cons.1: the ESD value depends on the printing temperature
entry.esd.cons.2: carbon-nanotube/carbon-black filler: needs a hardened nozzle
entry.cleaning.name: Cleaning filament
entry.cleaning.summary: Not for printing: when changing materials or clearing a clog, it's pushed through and removes the previous material's residue from the nozzle.
entry.cleaning.printTips: On a multi-head machine it's worth keeping one material family per head (e.g. 1: PLA, 2: PETG, 3: abrasive/hardened, 4: support or TPU) – then it's rarely needed. Start at the previous material's temperature, then cool down to the new material's.
entry.cleaning.uses.0: switching between high- and low-temperature materials (e.g. PA-CF → PLA)
entry.cleaning.props.0: usable over a wide temperature range (180–300 °C)
entry.cleaning.cons.0: push through by hand only, a few tens of centimeters at a time
